comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C63 and C65 regarding cytokine detection in ECM by mass spectrometry. Both evaluations find this data supported and not questioned.

Both address claims C14, C15, C67, C69 about ADE emergence after LY removal and differentiation efficiency. OpenEval finds the flow cytometry and immunostaining data sufficient, while peer reviewers question whether LY treatment produces posterior endoderm or undetermined early endoderm, requesting more careful analysis of alternative fates.

Both evaluate Fn1 knockout embryo data (C34-C37, C58-C59). OpenEval finds the genetic evidence from expanded Cer1 domains and foregut defects strongly supportive. Peer reviewers find the data intriguing but limited, noting lack of follow-up on foregut formation, variable phenotypes across genetic backgrounds, and requesting more comprehensive characterization of gastrulation and endoderm formation.

Both address claim C12 about apoptosis not being the primary mechanism. OpenEval finds the Annexin V staining and caspase inhibitor experiments adequate to rule out cell death. Peer reviewers explicitly question how the authors distinguish between differentiation and survival effects, asking whether there is significant cell death at the LY dose used.

Both evaluate claims C5, C26, C27 about differential ECM composition and Fn1 expression. OpenEval finds the LC-MS proteomics and q-RT-PCR data convergent and supportive. Peer reviewers note inconsistency between the authors' emphasis on Fn1 in results versus more nuanced discussion of ECM complexity, requesting clarification on whether Fn1 alone explains patterning effects.

Both address claims C28-C30 about reciprocal Akt1-Fn1 regulation. OpenEval finds the q-RT-PCR and Western blot data supportive of this relationship. Peer reviewers' concern about ECM complexity and Fn1's role (concern #6) extends to these claims, questioning whether Fn1 is the key determinant.

Both evaluate inferences C58-C59 about Fn1 restricting ADE specification. OpenEval considers these reasonable mechanistic interpretations of the Fn1 mutant phenotypes. Peer reviewers find the Fn1 knockout data insufficient, requesting further analysis before accepting these inferences.

Overlapping claims C6, C31, C33 about Fn1 expression patterns and role in anterior endoderm. OpenEval finds the q-RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry data supportive. Peer reviewers question the emphasis on Fn1 as the key determinant, noting the authors' own discussion acknowledges ECM complexity.

Both address claims C8-C9 about PI3K inhibition blocking ADE with critical window during days 3-5. OpenEval finds the time-course experiments demonstrate specificity. Peer reviewers question whether this represents specific ADE blocking or general endoderm differentiation arrest, requesting more careful analysis of alternative fates.

Both address claims C3, C23-C25 about ECM1 rescue of ADE markers and epithelial morphology. OpenEval finds the rescue experiments and Western blot data strongly supportive. Peer reviewers do not challenge these core mechanistic findings, stating the paper adds significant new information to understanding endoderm patterning.

Both address claims C16-C18 about E-cadherin localization and EMT markers. OpenEval finds the immunofluorescence and q-RT-PCR data convergent. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these findings, which are part of the core mechanistic work they find adds significant new information.

Both address claims C1, C2, C13 about PI3K inhibition effects on ADE versus mesendoderm populations. OpenEval finds the flow cytometry and q-RT-PCR data demonstrate differential effects. Peer reviewers accept these core findings as part of the significant new information, though they question the identity of alternative fates in R1.

Both address claims C19-C20 about correlation between Gsc expression, pAkt1 levels, and lineage identity. OpenEval finds the Western blot and q-RT-PCR from sorted populations supportive. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings.

Both address claims C21-C22 about Tamoxifen-induced Akt1 rescue and non-autonomous activity. OpenEval finds the flow cytometry and co-culture experiments provide strong evidence. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these findings.

Both address claims C4, C7 about ECM patterning cells independently of active PI3K/Akt1. OpenEval finds this strongly supported by rescue experiments. Peer reviewers accept these core mechanistic findings.

Both address claims C10-C11 about pAkt1 dynamics shown by Western blot time-course. OpenEval finds this data adequate. Peer reviewers do not challenge the pAkt1 dynamics data itself, though they question the apoptosis analysis (C12) separately in R2.
Both address claim C32 about ex vivo embryo culture with LY treatment. OpenEval finds this strengthens biological relevance. Peer reviewers do not challenge this finding.
Both address claim C50 about PI3K regulating EMT to control Fn1 levels. OpenEval finds this integrative inference well-grounded. Peer reviewers do not challenge this interpretation.

Both address claim C56 about no gastrulation phenotype in Fn mutants. OpenEval categorizes this as established literature knowledge appropriately supported by citations. Peer reviewers directly challenge this, stating the authors' own data showing Cer1 expansion contradicts this claim and constitutes a gastrulation phenotype.
OpenEval identifies claims C62 and C70 as explicitly speculative and untested hypotheses. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific speculative claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C51 and C71 as reasonable inferences about signaling context-dependence based on ECM rescue data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these broader conceptual claims.

OpenEval groups claims C38-C49, C52-C55, C57, C60-C61, C64, C66, C68 as established literature knowledge appropriately supported by citations. Peer reviewers do not systematically evaluate these background/contextual claims, except for C56 (addressed separately) and C68 (included in R1 but not specifically challenged).
